body:
Why Gujarat is important in Indian prehistory

Gujarat contains evidence of prehistoric communities that lived in river valleys, open plains and semi-arid landscapes.

Stone-tool discoveries in the state include Palaeolithic and Mesolithic traditions. Mesolithic sites in north Gujarat are particularly important for understanding hunter-gatherer life and the gradual interaction of such communities with later food-producing groups.

Langhnaj and Loteshwar are two important places to remember.

Langhnaj: a major Mesolithic site

Langhnaj is situated in the Mehsana district of north Gujarat.

It is associated with Mesolithic occupation and microlithic stone-tool traditions.

Important discoveries

The archaeological remains from Langhnaj include:

  • Small stone tools belonging to microlithic traditions.
  • Human skeletal remains associated with burials.
  • Bones of wild animals.
  • Additional material from different occupation levels, including pottery fragments.

The combination of microliths, animal remains and burials provides evidence of the activities and social life of communities living in the region.

What Langhnaj reveals about livelihood

Wild animal remains indicate that hunting was an important activity. Microliths demonstrate the use of specialised small stone tools.

The presence of human burials shows that the site was associated with more than tool manufacture alone.

Because Langhnaj contains remains from different occupation levels, objects belonging to later phases should not automatically be assigned to its earliest Mesolithic occupation.

Loteshwar: Mesolithic occupation in north Gujarat

Loteshwar is located in the Patan district of Gujarat, near the Khari River.

The archaeological site is situated on a sand dune and contains evidence of occupation during more than one cultural period.

Mesolithic evidence

The Mesolithic occupation at Loteshwar is associated with:

  • Geometric and non-geometric microlithic tools.
  • Stone-working remains.
  • Animal remains.
  • Grinding or working stones.

These remains indicate the presence of a microlith-using community that exploited the resources of the surrounding environment.

Later occupation

Loteshwar also contains a later Chalcolithic occupation phase associated with different material remains.

The Chalcolithic, or Copper-Stone Age, is a later cultural phase in which copper and stone objects were used. Its presence at Loteshwar does not make the earlier microlithic occupation Chalcolithic.

Other Palaeolithic evidence in Gujarat

Gujarat also has evidence relevant to the earlier phases of the Stone Age.

Orsang region

The Orsang region is associated with Middle Palaeolithic stone-tool evidence. Its inclusion demonstrates that Gujarat's prehistoric record extends beyond the better-known Mesolithic sites.

Visadi

Visadi, in the Vadodara region, is among the Gujarat localities associated with Upper Palaeolithic blade and burin traditions.

Important Gujarat site associations

Site or regionLocationPrincipal association
LanghnajMehsana districtMesolithic microliths, burials and wild animal remains
LoteshwarPatan districtMesolithic occupation followed by a later Chalcolithic phase
Orsang regionGujaratMiddle Palaeolithic tools
VisadiVadodara regionUpper Palaeolithic blade and burin traditions

Gujarat and the transition in prehistoric livelihoods

Mesolithic communities in north Gujarat occupied landscapes where water availability, vegetation and animal resources could change seasonally.

Microlithic technology helped people exploit such resources. Evidence from some north Gujarat sites also indicates the presence of domesticated animals, although the nature and timing of domestication differ between sites and phases.

These discoveries demonstrate that hunting-gathering and food-producing traditions did not necessarily replace one another immediately.

Prelims focus

  • Langhnaj is an important Mesolithic site in Mehsana district, Gujarat.
  • Langhnaj has yielded microliths, human burials and wild animal remains.
  • Loteshwar is situated in Patan district, near the Khari River.
  • Loteshwar contains an earlier Mesolithic occupation and a later Chalcolithic occupation.
  • The Orsang region is associated with Middle Palaeolithic evidence.
  • Visadi is associated with Upper Palaeolithic tool traditions.
  • Trap: A site with later pottery or copper objects should not automatically be classified as wholly Chalcolithic if an earlier Mesolithic occupation is also present.

[INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Mesolithic Cultures of India, sections on subsistence, settlement patterns and Langhnaj, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Outlines of Indian History, Pre-historic Cultures in India, sections 3.2–4, consulted 17 November 2026; Antiquity Project Gallery, Social and Environmental Transitions in Arid Zones: The North Gujarat Archaeological Project, discussion of Loteshwar and its Mesolithic and Chalcolithic deposits, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Loteshwar has an earlier Mesolithic occupation with microliths and a later Chalcolithic occupation with pottery: the same site, different cultural phases.
pictures.caption: The main distinction between the earlier Mesolithic and later Chalcolithic occupation at Loteshwar.

title: Prehistoric Gujarat: Langhnaj, Loteshwar and Other Stone Age Evidence

body:
What is prehistoric rock art?

Prehistoric rock art consists of pictures, designs or markings made on natural rock surfaces before the historical period.

Rock paintings are particularly important because they provide visual evidence of animals, people, activities and aspects of social life that are not always directly represented by stone tools.

Prehistoric paintings have been found in several regions of India, especially in Madhya Pradesh and adjoining areas of Uttar Pradesh.

Bhimbetka: a major prehistoric rock-art site

The Bhimbetka Rock Shelters are located in Madhya Pradesh, near Bhopal, in the foothills of the Vindhyan Mountains.

The landscape contains numerous natural rock shelters and evidence of human occupation over a long period.

V. S. Wakankar recognised the importance of the Bhimbetka rock shelters in 1957–58.

Bhimbetka was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003.

The site is particularly significant for its combination of prehistoric occupation evidence and paintings extending across several cultural periods.

What the paintings depict

The paintings at Bhimbetka show a wide variety of subjects connected with human activities and the natural environment.

  • Animals: deer, elephants, bison, wild boar, rhinoceroses and other animals.
  • Hunting: groups of people carrying implements such as bows, arrows and spears.
  • Fishing and food collection: activities associated with obtaining food.
  • Social activities: dancing, music, groups of people and scenes of daily life.
  • Human figures: people shown individually or participating in group activities.

Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic paintings

Indian rock paintings are associated with several prehistoric phases. Their appearance, subjects and composition vary.

Upper Palaeolithic paintings

The NCERT art-history classification includes an Upper Palaeolithic phase of rock painting at Bhimbetka.

This phase is described as containing relatively large animal representations, including bison, elephants and other wild animals, along with simpler human figures.

Mesolithic paintings

Many paintings at Bhimbetka belong to the Mesolithic tradition. These are especially important for understanding hunter-gatherer activities.

Mesolithic compositions often contain smaller figures and more elaborate scenes of human activity.

Group hunting scenes show people using weapons and sometimes traps or snares. Other paintings depict dancing, gathering and social activities.

Animals are often represented with recognisable physical features, while human figures are frequently more simplified.

Not every Bhimbetka painting is Mesolithic

Bhimbetka contains paintings associated with different periods, including prehistoric and later historical phases. The presence of rock art at Bhimbetka therefore does not mean that every painting belongs to the Mesolithic.

Although some early paintings are assigned to the Upper Palaeolithic in the NCERT classification, the precise dating of individual early paintings can be uncertain. UNESCO's site description emphasises paintings appearing to date from the Mesolithic onward.

Colours used in prehistoric paintings

Prehistoric artists obtained pigments from naturally available minerals and other materials.

At Bhimbetka, red and white were particularly important colours.

  • Red: commonly obtained from haematite or red ochre, also known as geru.
  • White: could be obtained from minerals such as limestone.
  • Other colours: yellow, green, black and additional shades were also used.

Some pigments may have been mixed with water and natural binding substances such as plant gum or animal fat before being applied to rock surfaces.

Another important rock-art site: Lakhudiyar

Lakhudiyar is situated in Uttarakhand, near Almora.

Its prehistoric paintings include human figures, animals and geometric designs.

A particularly recognisable theme is a group of hand-linked dancing human figures.

Lakhudiyar demonstrates that prehistoric rock art was not confined to Bhimbetka or Madhya Pradesh.

What rock paintings reveal and what remains uncertain

Rock paintings provide evidence of the animals people observed, the tools they represented and activities such as hunting or dancing.

They also indicate an ability to represent experiences visually and express aspects of social life.

However, the exact purpose of every painting cannot be established. Some may have represented daily life, social activities or beliefs, but a particular religious or ceremonial meaning should not be treated as certain without supporting evidence.

Prelims focus

  • Bhimbetka is located in Madhya Pradesh, in the Vindhyan region.
  • V. S. Wakankar recognised the Bhimbetka rock shelters in 1957–58.
  • Bhimbetka became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.
  • Mesolithic rock paintings often depict hunting groups, animals, dancing and other human activities.
  • Red ochre or haematite was an important prehistoric painting pigment.
  • Lakhudiyar in Uttarakhand is associated with prehistoric paintings, including hand-linked dancing figures.
  • Trap: Bhimbetka paintings belong to several periods; they are not all Mesolithic.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Prehistoric Rock Paintings, pp. 1–7, particularly the sections on Bhimbetka, Upper Palaeolithic Period and Mesolithic Period; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 18–19; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka, World Heritage List entry 925, description and inscription details, consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Prehistoric Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka, account of tools and rock paintings, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Reconstruction of prehistoric painting activity in a central Indian rock shelter.

title: Prehistoric Rock Art: Bhimbetka and the Cultural Life of Hunter-Gatherers

body:
The main changes across prehistoric cultures

The Palaeolithic and Mesolithic periods are related phases in the long history of human adaptation.

Both were characterised by a substantial dependence on wild food resources. Their most useful distinctions concern the characteristic tools, environmental conditions, settlement patterns and cultural remains.

How the tools differ

In the Lower Palaeolithic, large core implements such as handaxes and cleavers were important.

The Middle Palaeolithic is commonly associated with smaller flake-based tools, including scrapers and points.

In the Upper Palaeolithic, blades and specialised implements such as burins and borers became prominent.

In the Mesolithic, very small tools called microliths were widely used, including geometric forms such as triangles, trapezes and lunates. These could be incorporated into composite implements.

These distinctions describe dominant technologies, not completely separate collections of tools with no overlap.

How livelihood and settlement changed

Palaeolithic communities mainly depended on hunting, gathering and other naturally available food resources. Their movements reflected the availability of water, animals and edible plants.

Mesolithic communities continued hunting and gathering but adapted to environmental changes. Fishing, collection of wild grains and exploitation of varied local resources were important in suitable settings.

Some Mesolithic locations show repeated occupation, evidence of simple huts and human burials. In certain regions, domesticated animals also appear within Mesolithic or later occupation sequences.

These developments indicate increasing diversity in ways of life rather than an immediate, universal shift to agriculture.

Important distinctions for interpreting archaeological facts

Hunting and gathering versus food production

Collecting wild grains or hunting wild cattle does not itself prove cultivation or herding. Food production involves deliberately growing plants or managing domesticated animals.

Microlith versus composite tool

A microlith is the small stone implement itself. A composite tool is a complete implement made by combining components, such as a wooden shaft and one or more microliths.

Habitation site versus factory site

A habitation site shows evidence of occupation. A factory site shows evidence of tool manufacture. A habitation-cum-factory site contains evidence of both activities.

Seasonal occupation versus permanent settlement

A seasonal camp may be occupied repeatedly without being continuously inhabited throughout the year. Permanent settlement implies a more sustained residential pattern.

Rock paintings versus stone-tool evidence

Stone tools directly demonstrate technological activities. Rock paintings can depict animals, human activities and social scenes. Both are important forms of prehistoric evidence, but neither can answer every question about prehistoric society on its own.

Important places and their associations

LoteshwarGujaratMesolithic occupation followed by Chalcolithic occupation

Important conclusions

The Stone Age sequence shows changes in the ways prehistoric communities made tools and used natural resources. It is not a simple story in which every new period completely eliminated the practices of the previous one.

Hunting and gathering persisted in many places even after farming began elsewhere. Likewise, older stone-tool forms continued to be used alongside newer technologies.

Archaeological sites may contain material from several periods. Therefore, the correct association of a site with a particular culture often depends on the occupation phase being described.

Prelims focus

  • The chronological order is Lower Palaeolithic, Middle Palaeolithic, Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic.
  • Handaxes and cleavers, flakes and scrapers, blades and burins, and microliths are the characteristic tool associations to distinguish.
  • Mesolithic microliths commonly include triangles, trapezes and lunates.
  • Bhimbetka is an important prehistoric rock-shelter and rock-art site in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Langhnaj and Loteshwar are important Gujarat sites associated with Mesolithic occupation.
  • Mesolithic hunting-gathering communities could coexist with or gradually adopt elements of later food-producing traditions.
  • Trap: Neither a single small stone tool nor a later object from a multi-period site is sufficient by itself to assign the entire site to one cultural phase.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, On the Trail of the Earliest People, pp. 11–21, and Chapter 3, From Gathering to Growing Food, pp. 22–27; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Prehistoric Rock Paintings, pp. 1–7; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, modules on Lower Palaeolithic, Middle Palaeolithic, Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic Cultures of India, consulted 17 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Prehistoric Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka, consulted 17 November 2026; Antiquity Project Gallery, Social and Environmental Transitions in Arid Zones: The North Gujarat Archaeological Project, Loteshwar section, consulted 17 November 2026.]
